newsitem.title: UK: EMS/Mark stalls, German data highlights budget woe.
newsitem.headline: EMS/Mark stalls, German data highlights budget woe.

text.p: The mark was stymied on its European crosses, with a bias towards softness, after a report showed German joblessness rose in May in line with leaks.
The seasonally-adjusted German jobless total rose by 56,000 in May to 4.358 million, but showing a drop in the unemployment rate to 11.1 percent from 11.3 percent.
A separate report released by the Bundesbank, however, showed the unemployment rate rose to 11.4 percent from 11.2 percent during the month.

Immediate reaction to the report was muted. Still, traders expect the mark to cede ground in the coming days as the data highlighted the difficulties Bonn faces in getting its budget deficit down before the start of European economic and monetary union.

"The data was leaked so it wasn't a great surprise, but it does bring the focus back to the whole budget discussion," said Chris Tinker, the chief treasury economist at Standard Chartered. "The tone towards Europe has been more negative recently and the mark is being weighed down within that."
Mark/French franc was quoted at 3.3728/33 at 0921 GMT from 3.3716/21 late Thursday in Europe. Mark/lira was at 981.60/90 and mark/peseta at 84.41/43 from 983.00/50 and 84.47/48 yesterday.

Bernhard Jagoda, the president of the Federal Labour Office, said growth is not strong enough to turn the jobs market around and that he no longer thought the government's 1997 goal of 3.95 million jobless was realistic.
Jagoda also said Thursday that high levels of joblessness would lead to millions of marks more being spent on unemployment benefits than had been expected.

This reinforced traders' skepticism about whether German Finance Minister Theo Waigel can get Germany's deficit down to 3 percent of gross domestic product in 1997 in order to satisfy a strict intepretation of the Maastricht treaty's convergence criteria.
Bonn has had to back down from its plans to get a payout this year from revaluing the Bundesbank's reserves, leaving a 19 million mark budget shortfall for Waigel to fill from elsewhere.

"There's no change to a soft EMU scenario," said Adam Cribben, the assistant chief trader at Credit Lyonnais. "The German economy seems to be struggling to cope with the austerity measures they have already taken, and they will find it very difficult to get their deficit down."

The May U.S. non-farm payroll report published later today is expected to underscore the difference between German and U.S. economic prospects, and could undermine the mark against the dollar, traders said. This is expected to weigh on the mark crosses.
"The market is disinclined to change its position of being long of dollars at the moment," said Tinker at Standard Chartered.

Elsewhere, the Irish punt was mired near its recent lows against the mark and the pound as the country went to the polls. Recent opinion polls show Prime Minister John Bruton's ruling coalition government trailing behind the Fianna Fail-Progressive Democrat alliance.
The punt was last at 2.5645/95/58 from 2.6652/72 yesterday and at 0.9065/85 from the 0.9080 low it set yesterday. --Swaha Pattanaik, London newsroom +44 171 542 6284
